name: Negativland
label: SST
lede: Two Concord teenagers started cutting up tape in 1979. Four decades on, Negativland has faked a murder link to dodge a tour, been sued by U2's label and then by its own, and shipped a longtime member's ashes with a CD.

eras.title: Two kids, a tape deck and a midnight slot
eras.text: Two high schoolers in Concord, California, started cutting up sound in their bedrooms and named the project after a Neu! song. A late-night radio slot on Berkeley's KPFA gave it a broadcast outlet and, three years on, a phrase.

years.h: Mark Hosler and Richard Lyons name a band after a Neu! song
years.p: Both are still in high school in Concord, California. Their label, Seeland, borrows from another Neu! record: a track on Neu! '75.

years.h: The debut comes in hand-made covers
years.p: Every copy of the self-titled debut gets a numbered, hand-made sleeve. The band says it made 15,000 unique covers over 15 years: 9,000 for vinyl, 6,000 for CD.

years.src: Wikipedia: Over the Edge · Negativland: About
years.h: Don Joyce takes the KPFA board at midnight
years.p: Over the Edge starts in June on Berkeley's KPFA, Sundays right after Music from the Hearts of Space. Joyce hosts it for more than 30 years.
years.xp:
Callers phoned in unscreened sounds, rants and performances, and Joyce mixed them live with old radio, ads and his Booper, a circuit-bent oscillator.

The Internet Archive holds more than 1,300 episodes.

years.h: Third album, still on their own label
years.p: A Big 10-8 Place comes out on Seeland, four years before SST.

years.big: "The studio for the cultural jammer is the world at large."
years.h: Joyce's alter ego gives culture jamming its name
years.p: Joyce, speaking as his alter ego Crosley Bendix, uses the phrase on Over the Edge Vol. 1: JAMCON'84.

eras.title: Fire, then a hoax
eras.text: Escape from Noise nearly burned before it came out. When SST wanted a tour behind it, the band invented a federal agent instead, and the news ran the story.

years.h: The El Cerrito studio burns on Friday the 13th
years.p: The master tapes survive. The band rushes to Los Angeles to confirm the album with SST.
years.xp: It was a two-alarm fire that started in Smart Laundry, the dry cleaner downstairs; cleaning solvents fed it. The band got out with the finished masters and the artwork for Escape from Noise.

years.h: Jerry Garcia guests on the SST debut
years.p: Escape from Noise is Negativland's first record on an established indie. It also features [[Jerry Garcia|1ecff755-607d-4130-9a8a-8873f27e5de5]], Mickey Hart, [[Jello Biafra|2280ca0e-6968-4349-8c36-cb0cbd6ee95f]], [[Mark Mothersbaugh|6ff5f720-9fcd-434c-8a62-dc9dd123bde7]], [[Fred Frith|4801bad4-1b42-4c9e-84b1-bf61067ab67c]], [[Henry Kaiser|3b4ce4be-55a1-44bb-abdc-bcc504f30ca1]] and [[The Residents|8c9b336e-acc8-4e20-9195-6ed0634da9fc]].
years.xp:
Christianity Is Stupid is built on sermon samples from evangelist Estus Pirkle's 1968 LP If Footmen Tire You, What Will Horses Do?.

The original LP came with a yellow Car Bomb bumper sticker and a 20-page booklet of band history and reviews. A 1999 Seeland reissue has a new cover and the same audio.

years.h: SST wants a tour, so Negativland invents a federal agent
years.p: A press release says a federal official, "Dick Jordan," asked the band not to leave town: Christianity Is Stupid may have inspired David Brom, who killed his family in Rochester, Minnesota.
years.xp:
Neither Jordan nor the band's quoted attorney, "Hal Stakke," existed, and Brom reportedly owned no Negativland music. Most journalists were skeptical. San Francisco's KPIX ran it as news anyway and interviewed the band.

The Village Voice gave it two paragraphs: "their vagueness makes one ponder if this is just publicity." The band then declined further comment, citing its made-up attorney's advice, and put the coverage on Helter Stupid.

years.h: The hoax gets its own album
years.p: Side one takes apart the Brom story and the news coverage it got. Side two is eight versions of The Perfect Cut, built from a 1977 radio production.
years.xp:
Side one is two tracks, Prologue and Helter Stupid, running as one 22-minute piece. The samples range from Estus Pirkle to Lenny Bruce to a Charles Manson interview.

Robert Christgau gave it an A-minus.

eras.title: The letter U and the numeral 2
eras.text: A single that mimicked U2's sleeve got Negativland sued by Island Records. Then SST sued too. The band lost the record and the label, and came out with a book, a documentary and a standing argument about fair use.

years.h: Casey Kasem's outtakes ride a U2 song
years.p: Two takes on I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For, one laced with bootleg outtakes of [[Casey Kasem|9dd99129-8069-4528-b10d-5ca0179e42eb]] losing patience. The sleeve prints "U2" far bigger than "Negativland."
years.xp: Kasem's line on the outtakes: "These guys are from England and who gives a shit?" The tracks came back in 2001 on a compilation named after it.

years.src: Westword · The New Republic · Far Out
years.h: Island Records says the EP is bait for Achtung Baby fans
years.p: Island and Warner Chappell sue, saying the single is meant to confuse fans waiting for U2's new album. SST agrees to destroy remaining copies and, per Westword, pay about $90,000 in legal costs.
years.xp:
Greg Ginn's first response, per The New Republic, was that SST was putting the record out anyway. Then SST settled and announced it would recoup its losses from Negativland.

The band replaced the single with Guns, dedicated to "our favourite Irish rock band, their record label, and their attorneys."

years.h: Negativland prints SST's books and walks
years.p: The band reprints SST's financial documents in its magazine The Letter U and the Numeral 2, calls the label hypocrites and leaves. [[Greg Ginn|4f35de64-27ab-4426-95fd-8d454cda4e48]] answers with a press release and a breach-of-contract suit.
years.xp: Ginn told Westword the band wanted to skate off without meeting its obligations. In the final settlement Westword reported, Negativland got four SST albums back and Ginn got over $30,000 plus a live album.

years.big: "There's at least six records out there that are direct samples from our stuff."
years.h: Posing as journalists, they interview The Edge
years.p: Hosler and Joyce get the interview through Mondo 2000 publisher R. U. Sirius, then reveal who they are and grill U2's The Edge on sampling. That's his answer.
years.xp: The Edge also let on that U2 themselves were bothered by Island's legal action.

years.h: Fair Use: the lawsuit as a 270-page book
years.p: Book and CD tell the U2 and SST story start to finish, then add a large appendix of essays on copyright. Seeland publishes it.

years.h: Craig Baldwin films the culture jammers
years.p: Baldwin's documentary Sonic Outlaws builds around Negativland and the U2 case.

eras.title: Pepsi, Chumbawamba and a robot Lincoln
eras.text: With SST behind them, the band took on Pepsi, a radio chain and copyright law, then turned its own junk into a gallery show.

years.h: Dispepsi: a Pepsi collage titled in anagrams
years.p: The cover hides the name in case of a lawsuit. Once Pepsi's lawyers said they wouldn't sue, the band started calling it Dispepsi.
years.xp:
Fearing trademark trouble, the band first used anagrams like Pedissip and Ideppiss, ran a phone line that revealed the title, and worked it into the cover art through the design of the South Korean flag.

The samples run from cola commercials to talk radio, tabloid TV and the O. J. Simpson case. Critics split: Pitchfork gave it 4.0 out of 10, Spin 7 out of 10.

years.h: Ginn puts out a Negativland live album over their objections
years.p: SST releases Negativ(e)land: Live on Tour against the band's wishes.

years.h: Chumbawamba teams up on The ABCs of Anarchism
years.p: An EP built on Alexander Berkman's writing, with samples of Tubthumping, the Teletubbies theme and Anarchy in the UK, made with [[Chumbawamba|7b7b1e6f-e73e-41a0-9d72-8f0b30c6992d]].

years.h: A Clear Channel parody goes out on pirate radio
years.p: Negativland's send-up of the chain's stations airs during the National Association of Broadcasters meeting in Seattle.

years.h: Sued over samples, they help write the sampling license
years.p: Negativland helps draft the Creative Commons Sampling License, written to make sampling legal.

years.h: Twenty-five years in, a robot Lincoln
years.p: The anniversary show, Negativlandland, runs at Gigantic Artspace, 59 Franklin Street in Manhattan. [[David Wills|b57a41a4-7741-4ef3-9071-81d35217d681]], "the Weatherman," builds the hands-on Booper.
years.xp: The exhibit mixes artwork and video projections, with an animatronic Abraham Lincoln.

eras.title: Ashes in the mail
eras.text: Within sixteen months, from January 2015 to April 2016, three men from the band's past and present died. The survivors kept going, and packed some of Don Joyce's ashes into a CD.

years.h: Jon Leidecker, who records as Wobbly, becomes a member
years.p: After Don Joyce dies in 2015, he and Robert Cole take over Over the Edge.

years.h: Rivers Cuomo's 1993 song Negativland finally comes out
years.p: [[Rivers Cuomo|87b6344f-c874-49ce-a8b3-e467ed6e05d0]] released it on Alone III: The Pinkerton Years, 18 years after he wrote it.

years.cap: Mark Hosler at the 20th Olympia Experimental Music Festival, Washington, June 28, 2014
years.h: A Bible for a sleeve
years.p: The album about monotheism, It's All in Your Head, comes inside a King James Bible.

years.h: Ian Allen dies at 56
years.p: The former member dies of complications from heart valve surgery. His archival recordings turn up on 2019's True False.

years.cap: Mark Hosler at the 20th Olympia Experimental Music Festival, Washington, June 2014
years.h: Joyce dies of heart failure at 71
years.p: The man who named culture jamming and hosted Over the Edge for more than 30 years dies in Oakland.
years.xp: Joyce trained as a painter, with a master's degree from the Rhode Island School of Design, then worked in radio at KALX in the 1970s. He drew on Bob and Ray and Firesign Theater for the show's recurring characters.

years.h: Richard Lyons, the other half of the original duo, dies at 57
years.p: Complications from nodular melanoma take the man who started Negativland with Hosler as a high schooler in Concord.

years.cap: Mark Hosler at the Roter Salon, Volksbuehne, Berlin, September 2016
years.h: Two grams of Joyce go out with the CD
years.p: The first 1,000 CDs of Over the Edge Vol. 9: The Chopping Channel include two grams of Joyce's cremated remains, alongside 750 of his Fidelipac audio carts.
years.xp: The packaging got wide attention online. Ryan Worsley's 80-minute film How Radio Isn't Done collects archival footage of Joyce.

years.cap: Two members of Negativland at their electronics table, Volksbuehne, Berlin, September 2016
years.h: True False goes back to something like songs
years.p: A double album with song structures again, and Allen heard through archival recordings.

years.h: Surveillance and digital identity get the album treatment
years.p: The World Will Decide comes out on November 13. In 2021 the band plays an NPR Music Tiny Desk (home) concert.
